cards.title: Three components of a converting email: copy, structure, design
cards.summary: Break every ecommerce email into copywriting, structure and graphic design, then evaluate each separately against the goal of driving a purchase click.
cards.use_when: Planning a campaign or flow email (promo, launch, replenishment reminder) and deciding where a weak performer is failing before redesigning it.
steps: Split the email into three layers: copy (headline, body, CTA wording, social proof), structure (the order and placement of sections and buttons), and graphic design (buttons, colors, imagery, flow between sections).

Judge each layer by whether it moves a skimming reader toward the product, not by whether it looks impressive; the presenter argues brands lose revenue by caring more about how the email looks than how it performs.

Diagnose a low-performing email by location: if readers don't reach the offer, fix structure/button placement first; if they reach it but don't click, test copy clarity and offer framing; if it feels cheap or off-brand, fix design.
Make copy and design reinforce each other — copy should be scannable in the same rhythm the design implies, with bolded points and short lines rather than dense paragraphs.
Keep the design engaging enough that subscribers don't unsubscribe even when a specific email doesn't convert, since the presenter treats return engagement as part of the same asset.
caveats: The $150M revenue figure is the presenter's agency claim, not a benchmark for any individual store.
The presenter runs a paid agency; design judgment is his opinion, not a tested rule.

cards.title: 'Button at the top' rule for non-scrollers
cards.summary: Place the logo, headline, short copy and a large primary CTA fully above the fold so non-scrolling readers still have a path to purchase.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the hero section of any promotional or lifecycle email where you need clicks from subscribers who never scroll.
steps: Put everything a customer needs to decide at the very top: logo, benefit/pain headline, one or two short sentences of body copy, and the CTA button — nothing below the first screen is required to act.
Make the top button visually large; the presenter argues bigger buttons get more clicks and criticizes competitor emails where the hero button is small.
Treat the top block as an elevator pitch: it should summarize the single offer or benefit, not educate or list features.
Check where the fold actually lands on mobile in your ESP preview (the presenter reasons that most opens are mobile and non-scrollers never see below it).
Place the CTA button directly below the hero copy rather than after a graphic, so a reader who stops after two sentences can still click.
caveats: The exact fold position varies with device and ESP rendering; verify in preview rather than assuming a fixed pixel height.
Making every button huge is the presenter's stylistic preference, not a tested universal rule.

cards.title: Email structure: hero, bridge, repeated CTAs, footer navigation
cards.summary: Use a repeating structure — hero pitch with button, informational bridge with an infographic, benefit/product section with another button, then category-navigation footer.
cards.use_when: Building or templating a promotional email layout, or fixing an email where traffic stops partway down the page.
steps: Hero: headline calling out the pain or benefit, brief body copy, large CTA button, and a hero graphic.

Bridge: justify the hero claim with short informational blocks — the presenter shows benefit bullets, checklists, icons and ingredient highlights rather than paragraphs — and include a CTA button at the end of the section.
Add a final product or benefit section near the bottom with another CTA, so readers who scrolled the entire email still have a click target.
Repeat the button at the end of every major section, because a reader who finishes a section and finds no button simply leaves.
End with a footer containing 'shop by category' buttons (e.g., Men/Women) and additional links, to capture clicks from readers who reached the bottom but didn't want the featured product.
Use a strong us-versus-them or comparison block near the end when the product's advantage needs to be made explicit before the closing CTA.
caveats: The presenter's claim that category buttons in the footer recover lost clicks is his observation, not a measured result.
Too many buttons can dilute the primary action — choose based on the email's single goal.

cards.title: Make the email scroll feel seamless with gradients and flowing backgrounds
cards.summary: Use continuous background colors and gradients between sections so readers don't notice section breaks and keep scrolling into lower CTAs.
cards.use_when: Designing a long image-based email where readers drop off at section boundaries, or matching section backgrounds in Figma.
steps: Pick the main background color from the hero image or product photo so the palette is anchored to a real asset rather than chosen arbitrarily.
Keep a consistent background color throughout the email instead of alternating white and colored blocks, which the presenter calls 'blocky' and associates with drop-off at section ends.
Where two sections meet with slightly different shades, add a gradient rectangle that transitions from the top section's color to the bottom section's color so the seam disappears.
Sample exact colors from the image or existing brand assets using Figma's color picker (eyedropper) so text, buttons and background stay matched.
Repeat one accent color (e.g., the site's CTA red or an alert yellow) in small details — a discount bar, a 'last chance' label, button fills — to tie distant sections together.
Preview the full email scrolled top to bottom to confirm no visible banding between sections.
caveats: Gradients and background rectangles increase design complexity; the presenter uses a simpler first-pass layout before adding them.
The link between smooth flow and higher scroll depth is the presenter's reasoning, not measured data.

cards.title: Skimmable copy: pain headline, one-sentence body, three selling points
cards.summary: Write email copy for a three-second skim: call out the customer's pain in the headline, keep the largest block to one sentence, and sell on no more than three points.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing the copy for a promo, launch or replenishment email, especially when the current draft is paragraph-heavy.
steps: Open with a headline that names the reader's pain or situation — the Bite example asks 'What's in your toothpaste matters?' — then differentiate in the body copy (e.g., 'we'll never include harsh chemicals, plastic tubes, or toxic fillers').
Keep the largest body block in the email to roughly one sentence where every word is load-bearing; the presenter points out the biggest copy block in the Bite email is a single sentence.
Limit the selling argument to three specific points even if the product has more features, reasoning that readers can only hold about three things at once.
Move features into skimmable infographics — checklists, icons, timelines, short benefit labels highlighted larger than supporting text.
Use bold only on your own claims in comparison blocks; the presenter deliberately left competitor points unbolded in his ButcherBox-for-Pets build so the brand's advantages read first.
Structure the argument as: call out the problem, back it with punchy information, then tie in the product and stack the resulting benefits (e.g., healthier teeth, cleaner planet).
caveats: The 'three things' limit and 3-second attention span are the presenter's heuristics, not measured thresholds.
This style assumes a promo/consideration email; transactional emails may need more precise detail.

cards.title: Reverse-engineer competitor emails into a reusable copy template with ChatGPT
cards.summary: Feed a competitor email to ChatGPT, have it extract the structural template, then have it write new copy for your brand using that exact formula.
cards.use_when: You need fast email copy drafts and have identified competitor emails whose structure and angle perform well in your category.
steps: Collect a competitor email that you consider well-written and structurally proven for your market (the presenter uses Bite's email as the model).
Prompt ChatGPT to transcribe the email's copy into text.
Ask it to analyse that copy and produce a reusable template describing the structural formula (headline type, body sequence, CTA placement, proof points).
Supply your brand and product context, then ask it to write a new email following that exact template.

Let the model ask for the angle and positioning, then answer with a specific hook — the presenter used 'if your soap is white and perfect looking it's probably fake' with an 'ancient craft' positioning.
Review the output and edit before sending; the presenter says the draft took about two minutes and he would adjust details afterwards.
Keep the template on file so future emails re-use the same structure with different angles instead of prompting from scratch.
caveats: Treat output as a draft: verify claims, ingredient statements and any regulated language before sending.
Copying a competitor's structure is the presenter's recommended practice, not legal advice on copying their copy verbatim.

cards.title: Build emails as stacked image slices, not one giant image
cards.summary: Design the email in Figma, slice it into separate images for links and load speed, then stack them in the ESP.
cards.use_when: Producing an image-based email design and preparing assets for upload into Klaviyo, Omnisend or a similar ESP.
steps: Build the design inside a Figma frame, using roughly 600px width for the email as a starting dimension.
Draw Figma 'slice' frames over each logical block and export at 2x, so each export is a manageable file rather than one email-length image.
Slice by link destination, not just by visual section: because an image can only carry one link, split the footer logo, social icons and category buttons into separate slices with separate links.
Compress the exported JPEGs before upload; the presenter uses iLoveIMG's compress tool and reports one set dropping from 4.4 MB to 1.26 MB (about 72% smaller).
Upload the compressed images into the ESP and stack them in order, removing default image padding and side margins so the slices appear seamless.
Assign one destination link per image, and add brief alt text (e.g., the headline) for the case where images don't load.
Send a test email to your own inbox and check rendering and link behaviour before scheduling.
caveats: Figma's slice tool and ESP padding controls may change; verify the current interface before relying on exact menu steps.
Alt text is recommended but the presenter says he hasn't observed a clear deliverability impact from it.

cards.title: Hidden footer text to protect text-to-image deliverability ratio
cards.summary: Append a block of invisible body text at the bottom of image-heavy emails so spam filters see a healthy text-to-image ratio.
cards.use_when: Sending an email built mostly or entirely from images, where the HTML contains very little real text.
steps: Take a legitimate, on-brand text block such as your About Us copy and paste it at the very bottom of the email template.
Set the font size very small (the presenter cites size 5), tighten line spacing (he cites around 5%), and set the font colour to match the background so it is effectively invisible to readers.
Place it after the footer content so it doesn't interfere with the visible layout.
Keep using real, relevant brand copy rather than keyword spam, so the block still reads as genuine email text if inspected.
Verify the block doesn't break rendering or create extra scroll space by previewing the final email.
caveats: This is presented as a workaround that 'tricks' filters; it may violate ESP or mailbox-provider terms and could backfire if detected.
The presenter's claim that Gmail penalises image-heavy emails is his assertion, not documented platform policy; verify current deliverability guidance before adopting.

cards.title: Laying out an email design in Figma without advanced tools
cards.summary: Map the email as labelled placeholder blocks in a Figma frame first, then replace them with brand assets, so the layout is decided before detail work.
cards.use_when: Starting a new email design from scratch and you need to establish section order before choosing images and colours.
steps: Create a Figma design file and draw a frame of about 600px width and a height long enough for the expected copy.

Drop labelled text boxes for each section in order — logo, headline, body copy, CTA, graphic, sub-headline, body copy, infographic, CTA, footer — and size them roughly to the intended hierarchy (e.g., headline at ~30).
Use this map to decide section order and see the whole email at a glance; the presenter recommends this specifically for getting unstuck when you don't know where to start.
Import the brand logo and product images, dragging them into the frame; Figma shows centering guides automatically.
Paste prepared copy from a document, then adjust fonts (the presenter used Montserrat) and weights (semibold rather than bold) to bring the layout to life.
Build buttons by drawing a rectangle over the CTA text, grouping the two elements, and labelling the group (e.g., 'button one') so it can be copied and reused throughout the email.
Choose the palette after the hero image is placed, sampling from it, so gradients and accent colours match real assets.
caveats: Figma's menus and features change; verify current panel names if following step-by-step.
This walkthrough deliberately skips copywriting — bring finished copy into the layout rather than writing in Figma.

cards.title: Us-versus-them comparison block built with icon checkmarks
cards.summary: Create an explicit comparison graphic with checkmarks for your brand and X marks for competitors to make the product's advantages unmissable before the closing CTA.
cards.use_when: Writing the bridge or product-proof section of an email where the differentiator needs to be stated clearly (e.g., ingredient quality, sourcing, process).
steps: Place your brand on one side and a generic competitor label (e.g., 'most human-grade brands') on the other, using the logo and a simple 'us'/'them' header.
List your claims as short text points on your side and the corresponding competitor claims opposite; the presenter bolded only his brand's points to make them read first.
Add a checkmark icon to each of your points and an X icon to each competitor point; the presenter downloads free icons from the Noun Project.
Enclose each column in a rounded rectangle (Figma corner radius around 20) with a stroke outline, using a neutral background for the competitor column and white for yours so your side stands out.
Place the comparison in the bridge section, after the hero and before the final CTA, then repeat the CTA button immediately after it.
Keep the list short and skimmable — supporting copy above it should summarise the single strongest claim (e.g., 'not all human-grade dog food is created equal').
caveats: Comparative claims about competitors can carry legal and platform-advertising risk; substantiate any factual claim before publishing.
The presenter chose not to bold competitor points; this is a style choice, not a rule.

cards.title: Put footer navigation to work for non-buyers
cards.summary: Use the footer to offer category, quiz and social links so readers who scrolled past the featured product still have somewhere to click.
cards.use_when: Designing the bottom of a promotional email where the featured product may not match every reader.
steps: Repeat the primary CTA (e.g., a link to a plan-builder or quiz) as the lead footer element so scrollers land on the main action.
Add 'shop by category' buttons covering your main ranges so readers whose interest wasn't the featured product can still enter the store.
Include a small number of social links and a website link for readers not ready to buy.
In the Figma build, split these footer elements into separate slices so each button and icon can carry its own destination link.
Reinforce accent colours by giving the footer its own subtle background shape so it doesn't float without visual anchoring.
caveats: The presenter asserts this captures clicks from readers who reached the bottom, but provides no measured uplift data.

cards.title: Upload a finished image-design email into an ESP as stacked images
cards.summary: Set up a campaign, strip the template, upload compressed slices in order, remove padding, add links, then test and send.
cards.use_when: Publishing an image-based email built in Figma into Omnisend, Klaviyo or a similar platform.
steps: Create the campaign in the ESP, entering the subject line and preheader text (the presenter uses 'Last chance for 20% off' with preheader 'Open for your last gift opportunity').
Open any template to get a canvas, then delete the template blocks so you start from an empty email.
Add image elements one by one and upload your compressed slices, stacking them in the exact order they appear in the design.
Select each image block and remove image padding plus any frame side padding so the stacked slices align edge to edge and look like one continuous design.
Assign the destination link for each image — one link per image — and add short alt text describing the image.
Preview and send a test email to your own address, checking that the unsubscribe link is present (the ESP added one automatically in the walkthrough) and that links and rendering are correct.
Choose recipients — all subscribers or a specific segment with exclusions — review, then send.
caveats: Omnisend and other ESP interfaces change frequently; verify current campaign, padding and image-upload controls.
Sending entirely image-based emails means text-only recipients see alt text, so keep alt text meaningful.

cards.title: Image-only vs text-and-HTML emails: the presenter's position
cards.summary: The presenter argues image-only emails are standard practice among large brands and text/HTML is not required in 2026; treat this as a contested practice with real trade-offs.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to build an email as stacked images or as HTML text with styled blocks.
steps: Consider the presenter's evidence: he claims all of the 20-plus 7-9 figure brands he has worked with use image-only emails, and cites one roughly $200M/year brand doing so.
Weigh that against the costs: all content depends on images loading, so blocked images reduce the email to alt text, and text is not selectable, searchable or easy to edit.

If you go image-only, invest in the mitigating steps the presenter describes — compressed slices for load speed, alt text on every image, and hidden on-brand text at the bottom for deliverability ratio.
Still build a plain-text or HTML text version where your ESP supports it, so readers with images disabled get the offer and CTA.
Test rendering in your own inbox and in a preview tool before sending to the full list.
caveats: This is the presenter's opinion, partly informed by his agency's client base; it is not an established rule and contradicts common deliverability and accessibility guidance.
Image-only emails impair accessibility for screen readers and readers with images off — a real risk the source does not address.

cards.title: Compress and slice images to protect load time in the inbox
cards.summary: Keep individual email slices small and compress them before upload, because a single full-email image slows loading in the customer's inbox.
cards.use_when: Exporting a long designed email from Figma and preparing the files for ESP upload.
steps: Avoid exporting the entire email as one image; the presenter's stated reason is file size and slow loading in the inbox.
Slice the design into section-sized images and export at 2x for retina rendering.
Run all exports through an image compressor (the presenter uses iLoveIMG's compress image tool) before uploading.
Check the resulting file sizes; the presenter reports a sample set going from 4.4 MB to 1.26 MB after compression, roughly a 72% reduction, and treats smaller as better for load speed.
Upload the compressed files to the ESP and confirm they display at full width without visible quality loss or seams between slices.
caveats: The 4.4 MB to 1.26 MB figure is one example from the walkthrough, not a target threshold for every email.
Compression settings vary by tool; check quality after compressing rather than assuming it is lossless.

cards.title: Design principles that keep emails converting and subscribers subscribed
cards.summary: Use big buttons, matched accent colours, infographics and careful small details to make emails engaging without relying on flashy effects.
cards.use_when: Finishing or reviewing an email design before upload, especially when the layout works but feels flat or off-brand.
steps: Use large buttons throughout the email; the presenter points to Gymshark's oversized hero CTA as the model and says the bigger the button the more clicks.

Match accent colours across sections — the Gymshark example repeats green across image borders, callouts and buttons, and the presenter's own build carries the site's red through the discount bar, button and 'last chance' label.
Apply small depth details: a border and shadow on the button to give it a 3D feel, and a coloured border around the hero image so it pops against the background.
Use infographics instead of paragraphs — checklists, icons, comparison graphs (the presenter shows a graph making gummies look better than tablets) and highlighted key words.
Vary text weight (semibold vs regular, larger vs smaller) to create hierarchy rather than setting everything the same.
Add lifestyle or product imagery to finish the email and bring colour and realism into the layout.
Keep it restrained: the presenter's summary is to take the basics and elevate them rather than exploding the email with crazy colours.
caveats: Bigger buttons and repeated accent colours are the presenter's design opinions, supported by examples rather than controlled tests.
Engagement-focused design may not convert on a single send; the presenter frames it as protecting long-term subscriber engagement.

for getting unstuck when you don't know where to start.","Import the brand logo and product images, dragging them into the frame; Figma shows centering guides automatically.","Paste prepared copy from a document, then adjust fonts (the presenter used Montserrat) and weights (semibold rather than bold) to bring the layout to life.","Build buttons by drawing a rectangle over the CTA text, grouping the two elements, and labelling the group (e.g., 'button one') so it can be copied and reused throughout the email.","Choose the palette after the hero image is placed, sampling from it, so gradients and accent colours match real assets."],"caveats":["Figma's menus and features change; verify current panel names if following step-by-step.","This walkthrough deliberately skips copywriting — bring finished copy into the layout rather than writing in Figma."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","figma","email-design","creative-strategy","workflow"]},{"title":"Us-versus-them comparison block built with icon checkmarks","summary":"Create an explicit comparison graphic with checkmarks for your brand and X marks for competitors to make the product's advantages unmissable before the closing CTA.","use_when":"Writing the bridge or product-proof section of an email where the differentiator needs to be stated clearly (e.g., ingredient quality, sourcing, process).","steps":["Place your brand on one side and a generic competitor label (e.g., 'most human-grade brands') on the other, using the logo and a simple 'us'/'them' header.","List your claims as short text points on your side and the corresponding competitor claims opposite; the presenter bolded only his brand's points to make them read first.","Add a checkmark icon to each of your points and an X icon to each competitor point; the presenter downloads free icons from the Noun Project.","Enclose each column in a rounded rectangle (Figma corner radius around 20) with a stroke outline, using a neutral background for the competitor column and white for yours so your side stands out.","Place the comparison in the bridge section, after the hero and before the final CTA, then repeat the CTA button immediately after it.","Keep the list short and skimmable — supporting copy above it should summarise the single strongest claim (e.g., 'not all human-grade dog food is created equal')."],"caveats":["Comparative claims about competitors can carry legal and platform-advertising risk; substantiate any factual claim before publishing.","The presenter chose not to bold competitor points; this is a style choice, not a rule."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","copywriting","email-design","positioning","figma","creative-strategy"]},{"title":"Put footer navigation to work for non-buyers","summary":"Use the footer to offer category, quiz and social links so readers who scrolled past the featured product still have somewhere to click.","use_when":"Designing the bottom of a promotional email where the featured product may not match every reader.","steps":["Repeat the primary CTA (e.g., a link to a plan-builder or quiz) as the lead footer element so scrollers land on the main action.","Add 'shop by category' buttons covering your main ranges so readers whose interest wasn't the featured product can still enter the store.","Include a small number of social links and a website link for readers not ready to buy.","In the Figma build, split these footer elements into separate slices so each button and icon can carry its own destination link.","Reinforce accent colours by giving the footer its own subtle background shape so it doesn't float without visual anchoring."],"caveats":["The presenter asserts this captures clicks from readers who reached the bottom, but provides no measured uplift data."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","merchandising","email-design","email-structure","conversion-optimization"]},{"title":"Upload a finished image-design email into an ESP as stacked images","summary":"Set up a campaign, strip the template, upload compressed slices in order, remove padding, add links, then test and send.","use_when":"Publishing an image-based email built in Figma into Omnisend, Klaviyo or a similar platform.","steps":["Create the campaign in the ESP, entering the subject line and preheader text (the presenter uses 'Last chance for 20% off' with preheader 'Open for your last gift opportunity').","Open any template to get a canvas, then delete the template blocks so you start from an empty email.","Add image elements one by one and upload your compressed slices, stacking them in the exact order they appear in the design.","Select each image block and remove image padding plus any frame side padding so the stacked slices align edge to edge and look like one continuous design.","Assign the destination link for each image — one link per image — and add short alt text describing the image.","Preview and send a test email to your own address, checking that the unsubscribe link is present (the ESP added one automatically in the walkthrough) and that links and rendering are correct.","Choose recipients — all subscribers or a specific segment with exclusions — review, then send."],"caveats":["Omnisend and other ESP interfaces change frequently; verify current campaign, padding and image-upload controls.","Sending entirely image-based emails means text-only recipients see alt text, so keep alt text meaningful."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","omnisend","klaviyo","email-design","campaign-setup","checkout"]},{"title":"Image-only vs text-and-HTML emails: the presenter's position","summary":"The presenter argues image-only emails are standard practice among large brands and text/HTML is not required in 2026; treat this as a contested practice with real trade-offs.","use_when":"Deciding whether to build an email as stacked images or as HTML text with styled blocks.","steps":["Consider the presenter's evidence: he claims all of the 20-plus 7-9 figure brands he has worked with use image-only emails, and cites one roughly $200M/year brand doing so.","Weigh that against the costs: all content depends on images loading, so blocked images reduce the email to alt text, and text is not selectable, searchable or easy to edit.","If you go image-only, invest in the mitigating steps the presenter describes — compressed slices for load speed, alt text on every image, and hidden on-brand text at the bottom for deliverability ratio.","Still build a plain-text or HTML text version where your ESP supports it, so readers with images disabled get the offer and CTA.","Test rendering in your own inbox and in a preview tool before sending to the full list."],"caveats":["This is the presenter's opinion, partly informed by his agency's client base; it is not an established rule and contradicts common deliverability and accessibility guidance.","Image-only emails impair accessibility for screen readers and readers with images off — a real risk the source does not address."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","email-design","deliverability","accessibility","conversion-optimization"]},{"title":"Compress and slice images to protect load time in the inbox","summary":"Keep individual email slices small and compress them before upload, because a single full-email image slows loading in the customer's inbox.","use_when":"Exporting a long designed email from Figma and preparing the files for ESP upload.","steps":["Avoid exporting the entire email as one image; the presenter's stated reason is file size and slow loading in the inbox.","Slice the design into section-sized images and export at 2x for retina rendering.","Run all exports through an image compressor (the presenter uses iLoveIMG's compress image tool) before uploading.","Check the resulting file sizes; the presenter reports a sample set going from 4.4 MB to 1.26 MB after compression, roughly a 72% reduction, and treats smaller as better for load speed.","Upload the compressed files to the ESP and confirm they display at full width without visible quality loss or seams between slices."],"caveats":["The 4.4 MB to 1.26 MB figure is one example from the walkthrough, not a target threshold for every email.","Compression settings vary by tool; check quality after compressing rather than assuming it is lossless."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","image-optimization","figma","performance","email-design"]},{"title":"Design principles that keep emails converting and subscribers subscribed","summary":"Use big buttons, matched accent colours, infographics and careful small details to make emails engaging without relying on flashy effects.","use_when":"Finishing or reviewing an email design before upload, especially when the layout works but feels flat or off-brand.","steps":["Use large buttons throughout the email; the presenter points to Gymshark's oversized hero CTA as the model and says the bigger the button the more clicks.","Match accent colours across sections — the Gymshark example repeats green across image borders, callouts and buttons, and the presenter's own build carries the site's red through the discount bar, button and 'last chance' label.","Apply small depth details: a border and shadow on the button to give it a 3D feel, and a coloured border around the hero image so it pops against the background.","Use infographics instead of paragraphs — checklists, icons, comparison graphs (the presenter shows a graph making gummies look better than tablets) and highlighted key words.","Vary text weight (semibold vs regular, larger vs smaller) to create hierarchy rather than setting everything the same.","Add lifestyle or product imagery to finish the email and bring colour and realism into the layout.","Keep it restrained: the presenter's summary is to take the basics and elevate them rather than exploding the email with crazy colours."],"caveats":["Bigger buttons and repeated accent colours are the presenter's design opinions, supported by examples rather than controlled tests.","Engagement-focused design may not convert on a single send; the presenter frames it as protecting long-term subscriber engagement."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","email-design","creative-strategy","conversion-optimization","figma"]}]}

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the exact visual, structural, and copywriting frameworks required to build high-converting e-commerce emails, including practical tutorials on using Figma to design and slice image-based emails for platforms like Klaviyo or Omnisend. modules: [EML] topics: [email marketing, email design, copywriting, Figma, Klaviyo, Omnisend, conversion rate optimization, email structure, image slicing] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. email structure / positioning the headline, copy, and primary CTA button "above the fold" to capture non-scrollers immediately, followed by a "bridge" section with infographics, and ending with a footer containing category navigation; visual design / creating a seamless, scrolling experience using background gradients and dynamic layouts (e.g., S-curves, GIF carousels) rather than blocky, disjointed sections; skimmable copywriting / optimizing for 3-second attention spans by using punchy headlines, extremely short body copy, bolded main points, and infographics (checklists, icons, timelines) instead of dense paragraphs; AI copywriting workflow / using ChatGPT to reverse-engineer competitor emails by pasting an example, asking for a reusable framework, and prompting it to generate new copy using that specific structure; the "button at the top" rule / the strict design requirement to place a large, easily clickable CTA button immediately below the hero copy, ensuring it is visible without scrolling; footer navigation / utilizing the footer to include "shop by category" buttons (e.g., Men/Women) to capture clicks from users who reached the bottom but did not want the specific product featured in the email; Figma to ESP workflow / the technical process of designing an email in Figma, using the "slice" tool to export sections as individual JPEGs, compressing them (via tools like iLoveIMG), and uploading them as stacked images into an Email Service Provider (ESP); the "hidden text" deliverability hack / placing invisible text (e.g., the brand's "About Us" copy set to size 5, 5% line spacing, and matched to the background color) at the bottom of image-heavy emails to pass spam filters that penalize text-to-image ratios.

Look for.

The "Button at the Top" Rule: The non-negotiable design principle of placing a massive CTA button immediately below the hero text so that it is fully visible "above the fold" when a user opens the email on mobile.

The Invisible Text Hack: The deliverability tactic of pasting a large block of text (like an "About Us" page) at the bottom of an image-only email, changing the font color to match the background, and shrinking it to trick Gmail's text-to-image spam filters.

The Figma Slicing Workflow: The process of exporting a long email design into multiple smaller image "slices" to optimize load times and allow for multiple, distinct hyperlinks (e.g., splitting a footer into separate slices for different social media icons).

The ChatGPT Reverse-Engineering Prompt: The copywriting strategy of feeding ChatGPT a successful competitor's email, asking it to extract the structural template, and then prompting it to write new copy for your brand using that exact formula.

Skip. Plugs for the creator's agency (Well Copy), the newsletter sign-up pitches, and the extended, repetitive clicks during the live Figma design tutorials unless they illustrate a core concept.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (standard email marketing principles), 85% growth (advanced Figma design, conversion-optimized layouts, and technical deliverability hacks). Volume. ~450 words.
